30.q: No, neither was Jelly Roll's. Jelly Roll swore he's the composer of 'St. Louis Blues.' He said the old man stole it, he said, but since he made people think he did it, let him have the glory.

31.t: Jelly Roll Morton at the Lafayette
31.s: Hinton asks about Jelly Roll, and Whaley recalls him pacing in front of the Lafayette Theatre.
31.ch: Reel IV retellings and New York pianists
31.q: He used to pace around in front of the Lafayette Theatre, and Jelly Roll Morton -- so I'll come up to that later.

31.t: Jelly Roll Morton, the Lion's piano night and Joe Jordan
31.s: Whaley remembers Jelly Roll outside the Lafayette, piano night at the Famous Door with the Lion and James P. Johnson, Joe Jordan, and the need to read music.
31.ch: Coming up in New York and Harlem theatres
31.q: Jelly Roll Morton, I used to meet him in front of the Lafayette Theatre, had his music under his arm, walking up and down, said he was going to make it one day. Jelly Roll Morton.

32.t: Scott Joplin at Atlantic City and Alonzo Hardy
32.s: White says he knew Joplin, who brought four rags to the Jenkins band at Atlantic City and gave them to bandmaster Alonzo Hardy.
32.q: He came to the band in Atlantic City while we were engaged on the boardwalk there. Young's Million Dollar Pear in Atlantic City was where the Jenkins band was playing. When Scott Joplin walked out and brought his rag. The Maple Leaf Rag. Right. Then he brought- The first I ever heard of the Bolo…

33.t: Little knowledge of Jelly Roll Morton, and Whiteman's tune
33.s: DeDroit says he was too busy working to hear Jelly Roll Morton and says he was the only band to play a Whiteman tune.
33.q: I'm sorry to say that I had very little knowledge of Jelly Roll. He may have been the greatest. You see, my position is that I was working. And I knew what was around me. And I could only get a night off once in a while, you know, to go hear somebody else play. Did you ever hear A Sweetheart of…

34.t: Fred Washington, pianist who could read music
34.s: Pasley worked with Fred Washington at a taxi dancehall; they compare his reading ability with Jelly Roll Morton's.
34.q: Fred Washington? Yeah. Yeah, I worked with him. Yeah? Yeah, Taxi Dancehall, he's dead now.

35.t: Kindler's book and Bunk falling asleep to Jelly Roll records
35.s: They wonder what became of Kindler's book; Russell recalls Kindler playing Library of Congress Jelly Roll records for Bunk, who fell asleep.
35.ch: Move to New York and the Stuyvesant
35.q: I don't know anything about it. I think he finished it, and it was supposed to have been pretty good, but I don't know about the publication.

36.t: Jelly Roll Morton: style and personality
36.s: Morton was creative, ragtime-rooted, and got along well with the Red Hot Peppers though he argued with outsiders.
36.q: Well, Jelly was very creative. And he came up during the ragtime era. So I guess you would call his style more towards the ragtime style, you know.

37.t: Omer Simeon as an influence on white Chicago clarinetists
37.s: Chace feels Simeon's ease and ensemble playing foreshadow the hot Chicago style, and doubts that Jelly Roll wrote out the Red Hot Peppers parts.
37.ch: Teschemacher, Pee Wee, Noon and Simeon
37.q: Somehow I do, and I don't know why, really. But he attacked, he seemed to attack the instrument in a different way than Noon, or Begard, or Darnell Howard, with... How can you put it? What adjectives can you use? He had ease. He knew what he was doing. He was... He didn't... He doesn't ever sound…

38.t: Dance dates with Morton and Wickliffe's Milwaukee engagement
38.s: Levy played dance dates with Morton but no theaters. He also recalls Blue Mound Road in Milwaukee with Wickliffe.
38.q: Uh-huh, uh-huh. So, I was. Did you play any theater jobs? Oh, yes. I was. Did you play Milwaukee? Yes, I played Milwaukee. I was at Blue Mound Road with Wickliffe's Band. We had, we were spoiled at the.

39.t: New Orleans musicians in early Chicago and Jelly Roll Morton's arrival
39.s: Brown was a child around 1900; he recalls Jelly Roll as a loner who came up between waves of New Orleans players, and the Club Richelieu is mentioned.
39.q: I tell you, in 99, I didn't know, I was wearing short pants. Yeah. Wearing short pants. I didn't know much about anything. I was going to go to theaters.

40.t: George Mitchell and Jelly Roll Morton's Red Hot Peppers
40.s: He likes cornetist George Mitchell on Red Hot Peppers records; Crawford notes a growl on a tune sounds like Paul Mares.
40.q: Uh... Well, uh, I had one or two records with the, uh, the Hot Peppers, Red Hot Peppers. And, uh, this fellow that plays Cornet in their group, uh, a guy by the name of George Mitchell. He was, uh, he was a good Cornetist. I liked his style. And, uh, I'll say once before, he appears to be a…

41.t: Jelly Roll Morton records with the Rhythm Kings
41.s: Morton brought tunes to Paul, contributed to Milenberg Joys, and recorded with the band, a rare mixed session; Mares defends the band's Tin Roof Blues origin.
41.ch: Paul Mares and the Rhythm Kings
41.q: the New Orleans Rhythm Kings were probably the most popular jazz band in the country Jelly Roll Morton was just floating around and really couldn't get too much work around there and he was plugging tunes for Melrose Brothers Melrose Brothers asked Jelly Roll at least told him to go see Paul Merez…

42.t: Plans to hear music in New York, and modern players taking up Jelly Roll
42.s: He hopes to hear modern bands in New York and they discuss Jelly Roll Morton's compositions.
42.q: Good. I spent a couple of nights in New York, see if I can catch any music. I don't know. I was looking at the New Yorker, but I don't see too much on it. I'd like to hear some of the modern bands, you know, I mean, there's some who are interested in that as well.

43.t: Records for Victor and with Jelly Roll Morton
43.s: She recalls Man of War Blues and the sessions with Jelly Roll Morton, who knocked at the door during a take.
43.q: On Victor. But no, the Man of War was with Leroy Smith's piano player. What's his name? Let me see. If I can think of his name. Oh, I don't remember his name. He was a piano player playing with Leroy Smith's orchestra. Leroy Smith was playing then at the time at Shuffle Inn.

44.t: Jelly Roll songs and playing the dozens
44.s: Interviewer asks about Jelly Roll songs and the dozens; Welch recalls Jelly Roll Blues.
44.q: Yeah, it was a long time ago, the Jelly Roll Blues. Jelly, sweet Jelly Roll. You know, it was a record of Jelly. You know, I remember it now, but it's been a long time since I heard it.

45.s: Williams never saw or knew Jelly Roll Morton, though he was in California at the same time.
45.q: I never did see him. He was in California at that same time. He was there, yeah. I never did see Jolly Roll. I often heard of him about him.

46.t: Roy Palmer on records and High Society
46.s: Wynn and the interviewer discuss Palmer's reputation and whether he recorded with Jelly Roll Morton or played the High Society clarinet solo.
46.ch: Teachers: Preston Jackson and Roy Palmer
46.q: Yeah, Roy made a record, I understand, with Jelly Roll. I've never had to hear the record of High Society with Roy playing the Picou's clarinet solo. No, I don't think he did that. On the trombone.

47.t: Burton's account of a jam session at Paul Mares's house
47.s: Perhannis reads Burton's passage about a jam session with Mares, Bix and Wolverines; Moore does not recall it.
47.q: No, I haven't. Has he talked to you? No, and I'd like to catch up with him, I can tell you that.

48.s: Personnel recalled: Arnett Nelson, Harmon Edwards, Burton, Lee Collins, and New York sessions.
48.q: He was learning, you know, kids he was learning, but he was doing fine. A lot of those kids are smart, very smart. You just have to take pains with them though.

49.t: New York 1928-31 and Glenn Miller playing jazz
49.s: Asked about Jelly Roll Morton, Hazel recalls working in New York with Jack Pettis and a Pennsylvania Hotel band, and Glenn Miller's jazz recordings.
49.q: Yes, I do. Did you ever play with him? No, I never did. But I remember Jelly real well. I mean, more in New York than here. Mm-hmm. Because I was, I, I was in New York from, from, uh, 28 to 31. And that was just about the, the latter part of Jelly Roll Morton. Who'd you play with when, when you…

50.t: Jelly's personality, the diamond tooth and a family smile
50.s: She calls him colorful and egotistic, mentions misinformation written about him, and they compare memories of the diamond in his tooth.
50.q: He was colorful and opinionated and egotistic, he don't have to tell me about that, he is Egocentric, that's right A lot of the misinformation has been written about him too

51.t: Working and recording with Jelly Roll Morton
51.s: Ory recorded with Jelly Roll in Chicago only, and notes New Orleans had no recording at the time.
51.q: Just records. Just the records. Jelly never had a band. In Chicago he'd go around all the clubs and pick the men he wanted for recording. Yeah. Any records. Any records.

52.t: Jelly Roll Morton tour and records
52.s: Mason recalls roommating with Morton on an Ohio tour with Marable, the band's players, and the OKeh records made under Morton's name.
52.q: Well, I'll tell you, Jelly, Jelly Roll, my first meeting with him, he came to our band, came to Faith Marley's band to make a tour out in Ohio. About when? Yeah, that was in about 1927, I think. Yeah, 1927. No, 26 it was. Of course, and we were out there. He was my roommate, of course. We'd travel…

53.t: Jelly Roll Morton as a boy on the Gulf Coast
53.s: Billy says Morton lived with them in Bay St. Louis and traveled around Mississippi; as a kid he already played tunes he later recorded, such as The Pearls.
53.q: Well, he didn't come up here with us, but he'd go into New Orleans, and up and down the coast, Scranton, and, well, obviously. And then he lived with us, you know.

54.t: Ragtime tunes and Jelly Roll Morton lyrics
54.s: Interviewers ask about Erskine Tate, Maple Leaf Rag and Jelly Roll; he vaguely recalls hearing the words.
54.ch: Chicago and the wider jazz world
54.q: I don't know about the Maple Leaf, yes. I don't know about the Frog Lake, I can't remember. It might have been that, but it wasn't that Frog Lake here.

55.t: Sam Morgan band and Jelly Roll Morton
55.s: Brief talk about the Sam Morgan band and a dance hall job, and Bill never playing a job with Morton.
55.q: he had his head his own that old brass helicon on there the old brass so he did the horn do so George Foster was playing violin yeah he had his suit on and nice fella out I have seen him quite a while yes he's still in California did you ever oh did you ever play with the Sam Morgan band Sam are…

56.t: Jelly Roll Morton: Winin' Boy and his clothes
56.s: Ory describes Morton's walk, silk shirts, diamonds and pimping.
56.q: Yeah. No. I'd be dressed in the... His name was Winning Boy. That's what it is. Winning Boy, huh? Yeah. He used to wine when he walked, you know. You know, I kind of called him.

57.t: Asked to play Jelly Roll Morton tunes
57.s: The interviewer asks whether he can play any of Jelly's tunes such as Milenberg Joys and Wolverine; the rest is garbled talk.
57.q: Thank you. Thank you. Thank you.

58.t: Working with Jelly Roll Morton and dating Chicago bands
58.s: Punch recalls a year with Jelly Roll and places it after Tiny Parham and Hughie Swift.
58.ch: Jelly Roll, Leonard Reed and Chicago mixed crowds
58.q: Well, I didn't work with him but one year. Jelly got down sick or something, and the next year, I don't know, even Bain had this winter part, you know. And Swayze, he taken sick and died. And that was one of Jelly boozing him in, you know. And the other deal was blown in Chicago, playing different…

59.t: The Jelly Roll Morton album for Columbia
59.s: Sam Parkins' idea after the Joplin vogue; big band, small bands and trio with Venuti and Panama Francis.
59.q: Well the Jelly Roll Morton album for Columbia was Sam Parkins’ idea, the producer. And he thought, and he got Columbia to think, that with the unexpected popularity of Scott Joplin from the movie “The Sting” and the various recordings, including my own, that perhaps Jelly Roll Morton would be the…

60.t: Turk's love of Jelly Roll Morton and re-creating 1920s jazz
60.s: Turk brought out Morton's music; 1920s jazz had substantial writing compared with later New Orleans groups.
60.q: Well yeah. There are some things that were worked out. But I mean you had “Buddy’s Habits” and you had — the mind goes blank —

61.t: Listening to Jelly Roll Morton at Steve Smith's shop
61.s: Morton talked unappreciated to an audience of one; Avakian asked nothing.
61.ch: Hot Jazz Classics and how records were made
61.q: That was done entirely by gravity. I don’t know what formula they used to come out to – 78.26, I believe, is the standard speed – but that’s something that I could still find out about, because I have an old photograph of the man who became the head of the engineering department at Columbia Records…

62.t: Jelly Roll Morton as inventor of jazz
62.s: Wilson recounts what Duke and Mary Lou said about Jelly Roll Morton and defends Jelly Roll's claim to invent jazz as we know it.
62.q: the class because I try to keep it entertaining, you know. It’s really a great story when you tell the story of these guys, you know, and like everybody, this man is Jelly Roll Morton, I told you what Duke said about him, “Oh, Jelly Roll Morton wasn’t nothing.” He copied Jelly Roll Morton piano and…

63.t: The Wingy Manone record session with Jelly Roll Morton and Bud Freeman
63.s: Shaw recalls a chaotic unreleased date: Wingy sang the themes, Jelly Roll did his own thing, and later a tape surfaced; Venuti's cufflink joke.
63.ch: Early years: Cleveland, Aaronson, New York
63.q: Wingy went up to Harlem the night before, sat down with some arranger, and sang the themes to him. Then we got to the date. He couldn’t read, so he didn’t remember what he’d written. It was a mess of a date.

64.t: Jelly Roll Morton at the Jungle Inn
64.s: Taylor and other young pianists went to hear Jelly Roll Morton, who sneered at them and played in keys and styles none of them could match.
64.q: Jellroll Morton in I guess it was the late ‘30s, bought an interest in a club called the Jungle Inn. The Jungle Inn was right down the street from the Lincoln Theater. There were three… Washington was the capital of the United States but it was a very segregated town so anybody, Duke Ellington,…

65.s: Machito says Mario was wrong that he was there; "Tanga" grew from a vamp behind Miguelito's "Botellero" by pianist Varona and Mario's melody.
65.ch: War years, Decca records and La Conga
65.q: ....because they was accompanying Miguelito Valdes in "Botellero" - bran-baran-bam - a sort of vamp or botellero. Varona was the piano player in that particular time. You know, sometime you fake, you start to vamp and to filling in two minutes or three minutes because of the show

66.t: Visiting Jelly Roll Morton in New York
66.s: Before the Harris show, someone took her to Morton's office, where he roughly corrected her playing of 'Pearls'. She was not writing then.
66.q: No, I was only interested in him. I don't think I was writing too much then. I was just playing things that I heard or people were teaching me new tunes or things like that. I didn't start to write until I was with Andy Kirk.

67.t: Jelly Roll Morton at the Rhythm Club
67.s: At the Rhythm Club in New York Jelly Roll took a liking to Cheatham, played all his compositions for him, and recorded with him.
67.q: -- oh, that was gosh, that -- let me see -- that was after -- was that after? That was during the time of the Rhythm Club, I have to pinpoint that year. The Rhythm Club was in its heyday then, they had moved -- moved from -- it was on 32nd Street, 30 something street, and there was a guy named Hall…

68.s: Tate copied a few things from Morton but preferred Midwest and Texas bands.
68.q: : I listened to some of his records. We copied a couple of things from him, too. But actually, I didn't -- he didn't really knock me out like other bands I had really heard, you know, because they went together -- I liked that -- I kind of liked them arrangements and things

69.t: Was Tizol on Tiger Rag in January 1929?
69.s: Schuler suspects Tizol on the January 1929 recording; he doesn't remember and notes he played C trombone.
69.q: I don't know, because I know darn well even if I heard it, I don't know if I was not featured or anything, because I know well that on Tiger Rag, at that particular time, I couldn't even take no solos on Tiger Rag.

70.t: Jelly Roll Morton on the corner and his boogie-woogie story
70.s: Jackson listened to Jelly Roll Morton telling stories at 132nd and Seventh and recalls his claim that boogie-woogie was New Orleans race horse music.
70.ch: Harlem, Redman's band and the Savoy
70.q: Yes, I knew Jelly Roll. I used to listen at him standing on the corner of 132nd and Seventh Avenue and he told a lot of stories.

71.t: Trumpeter James Porter and 'King Porter Stomp'
71.s: He wonders whether James Porter, a fat little trumpeter in Mosby's band, inspired Jelly Roll Morton's tune.
71.ch: Freight trains and first trips to California
71.q: No, it was just a nightclub. It was a night club with a lot of chorus girls. But see, at that age I didn't, I didn't know anybody. I remember James Porter was a trumpet player. You know I often wonder whether James Porter was the guy who Jelly Roll Morton wrote 'King Porter' for. *

72.t: Brief dance tour with Jelly Roll Morton
72.s: About three weeks with Morton's eleven- or twelve-piece band in Florida and the East, for about $40.
72.ch: Postwar Chicago, Janis and De Paris
72.q: See, Jelly Roll Morton was only for just a few weeks. We did a tour, what's called a dance tour down in Florida, and so forth. That was after(?) ...(?)., played

73.t: The Rhythm Club corner: Jelly Roll Morton and Chick Webb
73.s: As a student he passed the Rhythm Club, remembering Jelly Roll saying he taught everyone to swing.
73.q: Okay. I used to go to the Lafayette theater, then the Rhythm Club used to be right in there. I used to come right past the Rhythm Club.

74.s: Mosley works briefly upstate with Morton, who carried cash, after meeting him at the Rhythm Club.
74.ch: Claude Hopkins, Fletcher Henderson and Fats Waller
74.q: I went with Jelly Roll Morton upstate and that was funny. He always walked around with a gang of hundred dollar bills in his pocket; he wouldn't be alive today if he was living.

75.t: Jelly Roll Morton at the Rhythm Club
75.s: Morton preached on the corner and held forth at the Harlem musicians' Rhythm Club, gambling and criticizing musicians.
75.ch: Piano craft and the New York school
75.q: : And the same thing with Jelly Roll Morton. He was unheard of. I remember as a kid where he used to be on the corner, sat on the corner and preach.

76.t: Jelly Roll Morton, respected and boastful
76.s: Zutty says Jelly Roll was respected though people gave him hell for bragging; his claims to know where Tiger Rag came from were credible.
76.ch: Chicago memories and the road to the Navy
76.q: Sure Jelly Roll was respected. They tried to give Jelly hell because he bragged so much. He could tell you where this came from. Where 'Tiger Rag' came from and everything. See, that's the kind of guy he was.

77.t: Trumpeter George Mitchell and working with Jelly Roll Morton
77.s: She recalls George Mitchell as tall and skinny and says she also worked with Jelly Roll.
77.q: Uh-huh. I don't -- George Mitchell. Maybe it'll come to me, but I can't recall right now. But anyhow, now we're going from the De Luxe.

78.t: Jelly Roll Morton at Bert Hall's Rhythm Club
78.s: Horace met Morton at the Rhythm Club jam sessions with Fats Waller and J. P. Johnson; Morton bragged he wrote King Porter Stomp and claimed he made Fletcher Henderson.
78.ch: Arranging for Fletcher, Goodman and Barnet
78.q: Yes. I knew Jelly Roll Morton. He used to hang around a place in New York City on 132nd and Second Avenue called Bert Hall's Rhythm Club where all the musicians hung out, and they had jam sessions there. They had a piano as you walk in, you know, and guys like the great Fats Waller and J.P.…
